title: Movable-type rack: lines typeset from a shared CXL slug case
idea: A print shop keeps one case of type and sets any page from it. Here a rack-level CXL memory appliance keeps one copy of each unique 64B line (a 'slug'), indexed by a 64-bit content hash. Each server's page table points to page 'formes', which are lists of slug IDs that the memory controller assembles at read time, with copy-on-write on stores. Read-mostly content (OS images, libraries, model weights, container layers) is then set once per rack instead of once per server.
why: Cuts capacity demand: rack-wide dedup at line rather than page granularity catches the near-identical pages that KSM misses, saving 1.3-3x footprint in VM, container and inference fleets that hold the same bytes in dozens of servers.

title: Roll-to-roll web: stream tiles depth-first through every layer
idea: Activations are treated like the web in a roll-to-roll line. Each input tile runs through all layers (or a deep stage) before the next tile enters, and the overlap 'splice' halos at tile edges are recomputed. Full feature maps are never written to DRAM; only a moving web of tiles stays in on-chip SRAM. The compiler picks tile size the way a line picks web width, trading halo recompute against buffer size.
why: Activation memory for vision, diffusion and video models falls 10-50x, and DRAM traffic for intermediate tensors (fact 5) mostly disappears, at a cost of about 5-15% extra compute.

title: G-code memory: store the toolpath, regenerate the part
idea: A 3D printer stores G-code, not the finished object. In the same way, deterministic data (positional-encoding tables, attention and dropout masks, index arrays, hashed embeddings, PRNG-initialized weights, procedural textures) is replaced by a 'toolpath' descriptor: kernel ID, seed and parameters. A tiny micro-sequencer on the CXL or DIMM buffer regenerates any line on load, and a page-table bit marks procedural pages.
why: Removes the 5-20% of AI and graphics footprint that is regenerable data stored for no reason; regenerating a line costs a few ns instead of DRAM bits.

title: Jacquard cards: KV vectors replaced by shared punch-card codes
idea: A Jacquard loom weaves endless patterns from a small deck of punch cards. Here each attention head keeps a learned deck of 4,096 KV 'cards' (a product-quantization codebook of about 1 MB, pinned in SRAM) shared by every user, and the KV cache stores only 12-bit card indices per sub-vector. The attention kernel computes q-dot-card once per card, then gathers scores by index.
why: KV cache memory shrinks 8-16x, and lookup-table attention is also faster, which frees the HBM capacity that limits batch size and context length.

title: Miura-fold addressing: store mirrored structures once, unfold in hardware
idea: Origami packs a large sheet into a small footprint using a fold map. An address-fold unit in the memory controller recognizes registered fold regions (symmetric, Toeplitz, circulant, block-repeated, palindromic) and maps each virtual access through a fold function, for example (i,j)->(min,max) for symmetric or (i-j) for Toeplitz. Only the fundamental domain is stored physically, and writes stay consistent automatically.
why: Saves 2x on symmetric matrices (covariance, Hessians, undirected graphs, distance matrices) and N-fold on Toeplitz and relative-position-bias tables, with no change to software that indexes the full array.

title: Zone refining: sweep high-entropy lines to one end of memory
idea: Zone refining drives impurities to one end of a silicon ingot. Likewise a background sweeper scans memory, measures the entropy of each line, and moves incompressible lines (encrypted, already compressed, random) into a dedicated 'impurity' region. The remaining pages become pure, zero-rich and low-entropy, so a cheap fixed-function line compressor gets 2-4x on them without a heavyweight per-page algorithm.
why: Page compression averages only about 1.5x mainly because a few random lines spoil each page; segregating them raises the gain on memory-expansion tiers toward 2-3x.

title: Die-cast slabs: address bits imply object type, headers vanish
idea: Parts from one die-casting mold are identical, so they need no label. The runtime allocates every object of a class (a 'mold') in a 2 MB cast slab whose address bits encode the mold ID. That removes per-object headers, vtable pointers and type tags, and 64-bit references become 32-bit slab-relative offsets decoded by a hardware base register.
why: Managed heaps (Java, Python, JS, Go) spend 20-40% of memory on headers and fat pointers, so removing them gives about 1.3-1.6x effective capacity for the biggest DRAM users in cloud fleets.

title: Sourdough starter: cultured dictionaries recompress cold pages
idea: Like a sourdough culture that is kept alive and fed, idle cores keep a per-workload compression dictionary that is trained continuously on sampled cold pages (zstd-style dictionary learning, refreshed hourly). Cold pages are 'fermented' by re-encoding them with the current culture. Old culture versions are kept so older pages stay decodable.
why: Dictionary-primed compression of 4 KB pages achieves a 1.5-2x better ratio than plain LZ on small blocks, turning a 2x compressed tier into about 3x with no new hardware.

title: Kanban buffers: memory scales with throughput, not connection count
idea: Toyota kanban caps work in process with physical cards. Per-connection pinned send and receive buffers (RDMA queue pairs, TCP socket buffers, gRPC channels) are replaced by a fixed pool of buffer 'cards' sized by Little's law: throughput times latency times a safety factor. A sender must hold a card (a credit) to transmit, and cards return to the pool when the data is consumed.
why: Servers with 10k-100k connections pin tens of GB in mostly idle buffers; kanban sizing cuts network and IO buffer memory 10-100x at the same throughput.

title: Wire drawing: KV precision drawn down through successive dies with age
idea: Wire is pulled through a series of ever-smaller dies. Each KV token likewise passes through 'dies' as it ages and as its cumulative attention mass falls: FP16 to INT8 to INT4 to INT2, re-quantized in place by a background kernel. Each die's threshold is tuned so the perplexity loss stays below 0.1.
why: Long-context KV is dominated by old, rarely attended tokens, so average KV width drops from 16 bits to about 3, roughly a 5x capacity gain on the same HBM.

title: Mine-tailings reprocessing: keep token IDs, recompute evicted KV on demand
idea: Mines reprocess old tailings when a new assay shows value. Evicted KV entries are discarded, but their 2-byte token IDs and a 16-bit key sketch (random-projection signs) are kept. When a new query's sketch dot product flags a tailings span as relevant, the KV for that span plus its neighbors is recomputed by a short prefill and spliced back.
why: For cold spans, KV memory goes from context x layers x dims down to about 4 bytes per token, a 100x+ cut for million-token contexts; the recompute cost is paid only when a span is relevant.

title: Interchangeable parts: snap near-duplicate float lines to standard gauges
idea: Interchangeable parts came from making every part to a gauge tolerance. A line-level 'gauge dedup' engine hashes float lines after rounding to a per-region tolerance, using a locality-sensitive hash on the top mantissa bits. Lines within tolerance map to one canonical stored line, while regions flagged as precise get exact dedup only.
why: Model checkpoints, ensembles, fine-tune variants, simulation snapshots and gradient histories hold many near-identical lines that exact dedup misses, so tiers holding them gain 1.5-4x capacity.

title: Intermodal containers: data stays compressed from SSD to SM register
idea: Shipping containers are never unpacked between ship, rail and truck. Define one compressed block format (4 KB blocks of individually indexable 128B compressed lines) that the SSD, NIC, CXL switch, DRAM controller and GPU L2 all understand. Data is then decompressed only into L1 or the register file at the point of use, and stays compressed in DRAM and HBM.
why: Today data is decompressed into DRAM, so compression saves storage, not memory; keeping it compressed in DRAM gives 1.5-3x more HBM/DRAM capacity and bandwidth for weights, KV and tables.

title: Group-technology cells: batch requests by expert-routing fingerprint
idea: Group technology puts parts with similar routings into one manufacturing cell. A router-predictor computes each request's MoE expert fingerprint from its first layers, and the scheduler batches requests that share a fingerprint. Each GPU then stages only a small 'kit' of experts in HBM, while the rest stay in host DRAM or flash and are swapped per cell.
why: MoE models normally keep every expert resident; batching by fingerprint cuts resident expert memory 3-8x, with high reuse of each staged expert.

title: Benetton postponement: dye per-tenant fine-tunes at compute time
idea: Benetton knits undyed sweaters and dyes them at the last moment. One base model stays resident and serves thousands of fine-tuned variants. Each variant is stored as a 1-bit sign delta plus per-row scales (or a low-rank adapter), and the 'dye' is fused into the GEMM, so no variant is ever materialized in DRAM.
why: N full model copies become one base plus N deltas of about 1/16 the size, a 10-100x memory reduction for multi-tenant fine-tune hosting.

title: Value-stream map: classify every resident byte into the seven wastes
idea: Lean value-stream mapping, applied to memory. An always-on profiler (page access bits, allocator tags, PEBS sampling) assigns every resident byte to one of Toyota's wastes: overproduction (prefetched, never used), inventory (cold for over 10 min), defects (leaked), overprocessing (duplicate copies or serializations) and waiting (pinned buffers). It then outputs a ranked kaizen list with automatic fixes such as madvise, compression, dedup and buffer shrinking.
why: Fleet studies often find 20-50% of DRAM cold or wasted; systematic waste accounting can recover about 25% of capacity without hardware changes.

title: Hoffmann kiln: compute wave rides the refresh sweep across banks
idea: In a Hoffmann ring kiln the fire travels around the stationary bricks. Refresh already opens every row on a schedule, so simple bank-level ALUs work on each row while it is open: scans, popcounts, zero-detection, dedup hashing, entropy measurement and scrubbing. Memory-saving services thus ride a 'fire zone' that marches through DRAM at no extra activation cost.
why: Background services such as dedup hashing and choosing cold pages to compress currently take host bandwidth; riding on refresh activations (about 46 fJ/bit already paid) makes them nearly free.

title: Quarry-side crushing: filter data in storage before it reaches DRAM
idea: Quarries crush ore at the pit so they ship less tonnage. Predicates, projections, decompression and vector-similarity prefiltering are pushed into SSD and CXL controllers (computational storage), so the DRAM buffer pool holds only qualifying rows or vectors instead of whole pages.
why: Databases and vector search provision buffer pools at 5-10x the useful data; pushdown cuts buffer-pool DRAM 3-10x for scan-heavy and ANN workloads.

title: Shift work: co-schedule jobs whose memory peaks are anti-phase
idea: Factories run shifts so machines never sit idle. The scheduler profiles each job's memory-versus-time curve (training forward/backward peaks, batch ETL, diurnal inference load) and pairs jobs with anti-correlated peaks on a shared HBM/DRAM pool, quickly swapping out the working set of whichever partner is in its trough. Pairing is solved like a shift roster.
why: Pools sized for the sum of peaks become pools sized for the peak of the sum, using 1.3-2x fewer GB per job across a cluster.

title: Sintering: press read-mostly structures into succinct form, remelt on write
idea: Sintering fuses loose powder into a dense part. A runtime detects read-mostly pointer-based structures (hash maps, tries, B-trees, adjacency lists) and 'sinters' them into succinct static encodings: Elias-Fano, rank/select bitvectors, minimal perfect hashes. Writes go to a small mutable 'green' overlay, and the structure is re-sintered when the overlay grows too large.
why: Pointer-heavy structures use 3-10x more memory than their information content; the sintered forms get within 10-30% of entropy for indexes, graphs and routing tables.

title: Freeze-drying: lyophilize idle tenants, rehydrate in milliseconds
idea: Freeze-drying removes water but keeps structure. An idle container, VM or LLM session is 'freeze-dried' by dropping all regenerable state (page cache, JIT code, allocator slack, KV that can be recomputed from tokens) and compressing the dry residue into a flash tier. An access-order trace is recorded so that rehydration prefetches data in the exact order the process will need it.
why: Clouds keep 30-60% of DRAM on idle or warm tenants; freeze-drying shrinks warm residency 5-20x while keeping wake time around 10-50 ms.

title: Retreading: remanufacture retired DIMMs into graded CXL expanders
idea: Tire retreaders reuse old carcasses. A remanufacturing line pulls DDR4/DDR5 from decommissioned servers, retests the chips, bins them by retention and speed, and remounts them on CXL expander cards whose controller maps around weak rows. The cards are sold as a warm memory tier.
why: Recovers hundreds of PB of existing DRAM from 3-5 year server refresh cycles, adding supply with no new fab capacity at an estimated 20-30% of new DRAM cost per GB.

title: Inventory carrying cost: bill cold resident memory like warehouse stock
idea: Manufacturers price inventory by its carrying cost. Clouds and internal chargeback bill memory by touched versus untouched GB-hours (taken from page access bits): untouched pages cost 3-5x more, and pages released to a compressed tier earn a credit. Teams finally get a price signal to shed cold memory.
why: Flat per-GB pricing hides the cold-page fraction (often 30-50%); a carrying-cost price signal could cut fleet DRAM 20-30% through behavior rather than hardware.

title: Rebar concrete: protected outlier rebar, bulk codes in 1%-BER cells
idea: Reinforced concrete puts steel only where strength is needed. Weights and KV are split into a sparse 'rebar' of outliers plus all scale factors, kept in a small strongly-ECC'd region (about 3% of bits), and a dense 'concrete' of 3-4-bit codes stored raw in 1%-BER cells. With outliers removed and codes clamped to a narrow range, any flip moves a value by at most one bounded code range, which is a tiny perturbation in a dot product.
why: About 97% of model bits move into cheap, unrefreshed or defect-tolerant cells while also being quantized 4x, so the high-grade DRAM needed for weights drops about 10x.

title: Lumber grading: bit-planes sorted into clear-grade and framing-grade memory
idea: Sawmills grade boards: clear wood for visible faces, knotty #3 for hidden studs. Tensors are stored as bit-planes. The sign and top two magnitude planes go to strongly coded memory, and the lower planes go raw into 1%-BER cells. The plane boundary is chosen per tensor so that the expected flip error (2^k x 1%) stays below the quantization noise.
why: 60-75% of each number's bits are low-significance planes where 1% flips add noise below the quantization floor, so high-grade memory demand falls 3-4x.

title: Vacuum pack with crash foam: compress pages, fill freed space with ECC
idea: Packers shrink-wrap a product and fill the leftover box space with foam. Each 4 KB page in the compressed tier is compressed, and the freed bytes hold a long LDPC/BCH code sized to the space left over. At page scale, 1% raw BER needs about 15-23% parity, so any page that compresses 1.3x or better carries its own armor at no capacity cost. Incompressible pages go to a small protected tier.
why: Flaky 1%-BER cells deliver DRAM-grade reliability for the roughly 70% of pages that compress, with net capacity still about 1.6x thanks to the compression.

title: Fan-deck ordering: codebook indices where one flip yields a similar shade
idea: Paint fan decks put similar shades on adjacent cards, so grabbing the wrong one still looks right. For vector-quantized weights and embeddings, codebook indices are assigned by simulated annealing so that codewords whose indices differ by one bit are nearest neighbors in vector space (a Gray-like assignment). Indices are stored raw in 1%-BER cells, and a flip swaps in a nearly identical codeword.
why: Makes 2-3 bit/weight VQ (5-8x smaller than FP16) tolerant of 1% raw BER with no ECC; the assignment cuts flip distortion about 5-10x versus random index order.

title: Batch blender: Hadamard-mix tensors so bit flips become diffuse noise
idea: Bulk blenders homogenize a batch so that no pocket is off-spec. Tensors are multiplied by a randomized Hadamard transform before quantization and storage, so after the fast inverse transform in the load path, one flipped value is spread at low amplitude across 256-4096 reconstructed values. The same rotation flattens outliers, which allows 3-4-bit quantization.
why: Sparse catastrophic errors become Gaussian-like noise about 1/sqrt(N) in amplitude, so 1%-BER storage costs only a small SNR penalty while the data is also quantized 4x.

title: Halftone screen: error-diffused 1-bit weights that shrug off flips
idea: Halftone printing renders gray with binary dots plus error diffusion. Weights are binarized with Floyd-Steinberg-style error diffusion along the input dimension, carrying each residual to neighboring weights, and per-block FP16 scales are kept in protected memory. Each output sums thousands of +/-1 weights, so 1% flips act as small additive noise, like a few misprinted dots.
why: At 1 bit per weight (16x smaller than FP16), stored in unprotected 1%-BER cells, the high-grade memory needed for weights falls more than 16x.

title: Felting: superpose many key-value pairs into one hypervector mat
idea: Felt mats thousands of fibers into one sheet with no single point of failure. Associative stores (retrieval caches, semantic caches, feature stores) bind each key and value into a 10k-bit hypervector and bundle hundreds of pairs into one stored vector by majority sum. A lookup unbinds with the key and cleans up against a small codebook, and the representation survives even 10% bit flips.
why: Holds hundreds of approximate associations per 1.25 KB vector, 5-20x denser than hash tables for approximate-lookup workloads, and natively immune to 1% BER.

title: Factory seconds: sell test-reject DRAM dies as AI-grade memory
idea: Outlet stores sell slightly flawed 'seconds'. DRAM makers take dies that fail JEDEC retention or defect screens but run at about 1% raw BER under relaxed refresh, and bin them into an 'AI-grade' SKU: CXL modules with a page-level LDPC controller, sold for error-tolerant data such as KV, activations and low bit-planes.
why: Recovers the 5-15% of dies that are scrapped or down-binned and lets marginal process windows ship, adding usable bit supply without a new fab at a lower cost per GB.

title: SPC control charts per row: data classes follow measured cell quality
idea: Statistical process control tracks each machine against control limits. The memory controller keeps a CUSUM chart of corrected and detected errors for every row (from scrub and parity) and classifies rows as A (<0.01%), B (<0.3%) or C (up to 1%). Pages are remapped so precise data lives in A rows, approximate tensors in B rows, and noise-tolerant data (KV tails, activation stash, low bit-planes) in C rows.
why: Cell quality varies about 100x across a die; matching data tolerance to measured row quality lets whole modules run at relaxed refresh or voltage with 1% worst-case rows instead of paying for guard bands.

title: Scrap remelt: near-capacity code, refetch master copy on decode failure
idea: Foundries simply remelt bad castings. Clean data that can be fetched again (page cache, model weights, container images) sits in 1%-BER cells under a near-capacity 4 KB LDPC code with only about 10-12% overhead and a deliberately high failure rate of about 1e-6 per page read. When decoding fails, the page is refetched from SSD or a remote master, which is cheap because it is rare.
why: Accepting rare decode failures instead of guaranteeing 1e-15 roughly halves the ECC margin, and lets the largest DRAM consumer, caches of durable data, live in cheap flaky cells.

title: Ripstop weave: error-contained compression for media and sensor buffers
idea: Ripstop fabric has a heavy thread every few mm so tears cannot spread. Compressed video frames, images and sensor streams kept in memory use fixed-length transform-coefficient codes and reversible variable-length codes, with a resync point every 32 symbols. A flip then corrupts one coefficient in one block instead of the rest of the stream, and the decoder conceals damaged blocks from their neighbors.
why: Camera, video-analytics and vehicle-log buffers can stay compressed 5-20x in 1%-BER memory instead of being decompressed into perfect DRAM.

title: Double-cloth weaving: cross-node erasure code replaces replicas and ECC
idea: Double cloth interlaces two layers so either one can carry the load. In-memory stores that replicate 3x across servers instead protect pages with a product code. A light inner LDPC per node (about 6%) cleans most of each node's 1%-BER flips, and an outer (8+3) erasure code across 11 servers corrects whatever the inner decode misses as well as whole-node loss. Per-DIMM ECC goes away.
why: Replication overhead drops from 3x to about 1.45x (about 2x less DRAM), the local ECC tax disappears, and cheap 1%-BER modules become usable.

title: Cored casting: coarse skeleton protected, fine interior repaired by physics
idea: Cored castings are hollow, with metal only where strength is needed. Simulation state is stored as a coarse multigrid level in protected memory plus fine-level residual corrections at 4-8 bits in 1%-BER cells. On each load, a local PDE-residual check flags any cell whose residual jumps (the signature of a bit flip), and only those cells are re-solved from their neighbors and the coarse level.
why: Fine meshes dominate scientific DRAM use; storing them as low-bit residuals cuts footprint 4-8x, and the physics itself detects and corrects errors at 1% BER.

title: Quench-and-temper training: harden models against the exact flip channel
idea: Steel is hardened by quenching, then tempered to remove brittleness. Models are fine-tuned with 1% bit flips injected into the exact stored bit format (the quantized codes, not the protected scales) using straight-through estimators, then 'tempered' with a short pass on clean data. The hardened model is deployed at 3 bits per weight on 1%-BER memory.
why: Fault-aware training is reported to recover much of the accuracy lost to flips, enabling about 5x weight compression on cheap unrefreshed cells and less premium HBM per inference server.

title: Fiducial marks: pilot-calibrated two-bit-per-cell DRAM with soft decoding
idea: Pick-and-place machines read fiducial marks to correct for drift. Each DRAM page embeds pilot cells with known values, read through the sense amp at several reference levels to track drift and leakage. That lets each cell hold 2 bits (4 charge levels), and a soft-decision LDPC decoder uses pilot-calibrated likelihoods to turn a ~1% raw symbol error rate into reliable reads for a compressed or cold tier.
why: Doubles the bits per capacitor, giving 2x density on the same wafer area and EUV layers for page-granularity tiers where LDPC latency is hidden; the 1% error budget is what makes multi-level DRAM viable.

title: Fettling attention: grind off flip burrs from KV before softmax
idea: Foundry fettling grinds the burrs off sand castings. The KV cache lives in 1%-BER cells as int4, with per-head scales protected. The attention kernel 'fettles' each key and value it loads by clamping it to calibrated per-channel bounds and capping softmax weights (top-k trimmed), so a flip that creates an outlier logit cannot hijack attention.
why: Moves the KV cache, the biggest inference memory consumer, to cheap low-refresh cells. int4 already gives 4x capacity, and robust aggregation is expected to keep perplexity within about 0.1-0.3 at 1% BER.

title: Andon cord: fast raw reads, full decode only when confidence drops
idea: Toyota workers pull the andon cord to stop the line only when they see a defect. Weights sit in 1%-BER memory under a systematic LDPC whose data bits are usable as-is, so the fast path reads only the data bits and skips parity. When the model's token entropy or logit margin crosses an anomaly threshold, the step is re-run on parity-decoded weights.
why: Gives cheap-cell capacity with no decode latency on more than 99% of steps, and limits quality loss to rare anomalous steps, at about 12% parity instead of duplicate copies.

title: Rotational molding: scramble stashed activations so flips average to zero
idea: Rotomolding spins the mold on two axes so material deposits evenly, with no bias. DRAM retention failures are one-directional (charged cells lose charge), which biases the value errors. Activations saved for backprop are therefore stored at 4 bits in 1%-BER cells, XORed with a PRNG mask whose per-block seed lets the mask be regenerated on read. A charge-loss flip then means +2^k or -2^k with equal probability, so the noise is zero-mean and gradients stay unbiased, only slightly noisier than SGD already is.
why: The activation stash is the largest training memory consumer; an unprotected 4-bit stash cuts it about 4x and moves it to cheap cells without checkpoint recompute.

title: Flour sifter: multi-sieve sketches replace exact tables, median rejects flips
idea: Millers sift flour through a stack of sieves. Exact counting and lookup tables (flow tables, feature-frequency counters, dedup indices, recommendation counts) are replaced by count-median sketches with 5 'sieves' of saturating 8-bit log counters. Taking the median across sieves rejects a counter that a flip pushed up or down, so 1% BER barely moves the estimate.
why: Sketches use 10-100x less memory than exact hash tables at bounded error, and the median turns 1% cell BER into a negligible error.

title: LEGO kit-of-parts: compositional embeddings from small shared brick tables
idea: LEGO builds endless models from a few brick types. Terabyte-scale recommendation embedding tables are replaced by compositional embeddings: each ID's vector is the sum of 4 vectors drawn from small 'brick' tables indexed by a hash or quotient-remainder split of the ID. A flip in one brick contributes only a quarter of the vector's error, and the bricks are trained with 1% flip injection.
why: Recommendation embeddings are among the largest DRAM users (multi-TB per model); compositional tables shrink them 10-1000x and tolerate 1% BER by construction.

title: Galvanizing: structure plated with protection, payload left raw
idea: Galvanizing coats only the surface of steel with zinc. A type-annotated allocator puts pointers, lengths, keys, headers and control state in ECC-protected memory, and bulky approximate payloads (images, embeddings, audio, ML features, KV values) in 1%-BER cells. Compiler-checked 'approximate' qualifiers stop raw data from flowing into addresses or branches.
why: Payload is 80-95% of the bytes in ML feature stores, media caches and key-value stores, so moving it to cheap tolerant cells cuts premium DRAM 5-10x.

title: Mass-balance reconciliation: repair flips by enforcing data's built-in invariants
idea: Chemical plants reconcile noisy flow meters against mass-balance constraints. Data that already carries invariants (monotone CSR row offsets, sorted index arrays, distributions that sum to 1, histograms with known totals, rotation matrices) is stored raw in 1%-BER cells. On load, a reconciliation unit finds entries that violate the invariant and resets them to the least-squares value consistent with their neighbors, so the data's own structure replaces ECC. Delta-compressing the monotone arrays saves 2-4x on top.
why: Graph and sparse-matrix index arrays are a huge share of analytics DRAM; they can be delta-compressed and moved to cheap cells with no ECC overhead.

title: Printing-house proofreader: language-model prior corrects flipped token streams
idea: Proofreaders fix typos from context. Stored token streams (prompt histories kept in place of KV, chat logs, RAG document caches, tokenized corpora) live in 1%-BER memory with only about 3% parity. On read, a small language model does joint source-channel decoding: for each corrupted 16-bit token it scores the roughly 17 one-flip candidates by LM likelihood times channel likelihood, subject to the parity, so the redundancy in the text itself corrects the errors.
why: Text carries about 1 bit of entropy per stored character byte, so using that redundancy as the code removes most ECC overhead; combined with storing token IDs instead of KV it supports 100x memory savings for long-context serving.
